s: A 52-year-old woman undergoes left mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection for invasive breast carcinoma. At her 2-week follow-up visit, the medial border of her left scapula lifts away from the chest wall when she pushes against a wall with both hands.
l: Injury to which nerve best explains this finding?
e: The **long thoracic nerve** (C5 to C7) runs down the medial wall of the axilla on the surface of serratus anterior, right in the field of an axillary node dissection. Serratus anterior holds the scapula against the ribs. When it is paralyzed, the medial border lifts off the chest wall as the patient pushes forward. This is a winged scapula. The thoracodorsal nerve supplies latissimus dorsi and causes weak adduction and extension without winging, and the intercostobrachial nerve is purely sensory.

w.Thoracodorsal nerve: This nerve runs along the posterior axillary wall to latissimus dorsi. Injury weakens adduction, extension and internal rotation of the arm, but the scapula stays flat.
w.Intercostobrachial nerve: This sensory branch of T2 crosses the axilla. Cutting it numbs the medial upper arm without any muscle weakness.
w.Medial pectoral nerve: This nerve supplies the pectoral muscles. Damage weakens the chest muscles but does not lift the scapula off the ribs.
w.Axillary nerve: The axillary nerve wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus to supply the deltoid. Injury follows shoulder dislocation or fracture and weakens abduction.

et: Skin of the medial upper arm
Around the surgical neck of the humerus
bl: Winged scapula after axillary dissection means the long thoracic nerve to serratus anterior was injured.

pt.say: The first nerve card shows the long thoracic nerve on serratus anterior, whose injury gives a winged scapula.

s: A 58-year-old woman notices a change in her right breast. Examination shows a 2-cm hard, irregular mass in the upper outer quadrant. When she raises both arms above her head, the skin directly over the mass puckers inward.
l: Tumor involvement of which structure most directly causes the skin change?
e: Fibrous **Cooper ligaments** run from the dermis through the breast to the deep fascia. A carcinoma that invades them causes scarring that shortens the bands, so the skin they anchor is pulled inward into a dimple. Blocked dermal lymphatic vessels cause edematous, pitted peau d'orange skin instead. Tumor in the lactiferous ducts pulls the nipple inward, and invasion of the pectoral fascia fixes the mass to the chest wall without dimpling the skin.

w.Dermal lymphatic vessels: Tumor in the dermal lymphatics causes skin edema and a pitted peau d'orange surface, typical of inflammatory carcinoma. It does not pucker the skin into a dimple.
w.Lactiferous ducts: When tumor shortens the ducts beneath the areola, the nipple itself is drawn inward. The skin over a peripheral lesion is not pulled.
w.Pectoral fascia: Invasion through the retromammary space into the pectoral fascia anchors the mass so that it moves with the contracting muscle. It does not pucker the skin.
w.Axillary lymph nodes: Nodal metastases cause a firm lump in the armpit and stage the disease. They cannot pull on the skin over the primary tumor.

bl: Skin dimpling over a breast cancer means tumor has shortened the Cooper (suspensory) ligaments.

pt.say: The Cooper (suspensory) ligament runs from the skin to the fascia; the note at the bottom shows that shortening it pulls the skin inward.

s: A 61-year-old woman has a 4-cm mass in the lower inner quadrant of her left breast. With her arms relaxed at her sides, the mass can be moved slightly over the chest wall. When she presses her hands firmly against her hips, the mass no longer moves independently and shifts with the underlying muscle. The overlying skin is smooth.
l: Tumor extension into which structure explains this finding?
e: The breast normally glides over pectoralis major because the loose retromammary space separates it from the **pectoral fascia**. A carcinoma that grows across this space and attaches to the fascia becomes fixed. When she tenses the muscle by pressing on her hips, the mass moves with it. Fixation signals deep invasion. Involvement of Cooper ligaments would dimple the skin, which is smooth here, and involvement of the lactiferous ducts would pull the nipple inward.

w.Suspensory (Cooper) ligaments: Shortened Cooper ligaments pull the overlying skin into a dimple, and her skin is smooth. Tethering to skin does not bind a lesion to muscle.
w.Lactiferous ducts: Tumor along the large ducts beneath the areola retracts or inverts the nipple. A peripheral mass fixed to muscle points to a deeper plane.
w.Dermal lymphatic vessels: Tumor in the dermal lymphatics thickens and reddens the skin into peau d'orange. That is a superficial change and leaves the deep gliding plane intact.
w.Internal mammary lymph nodes: These parasternal nodes drain the medial quadrants, but metastasis there is not palpable and does not change how the primary mass slides.

bl: A mass that moves with contracting pectoralis has invaded the pectoral fascia across the retromammary space.

pt.say: Tumor that crosses the retromammary space reaches the pectoral fascia, so the mass is anchored; the bottom note calls this fixation.

s: A 47-year-old woman is found to have a 1.8-cm invasive carcinoma in the upper inner quadrant of her right breast, 2 cm from the edge of the sternum. Before surgery, radiotracer is injected around the tumor. Lymphoscintigraphy shows a single deep sentinel node outside the axilla, and no axillary uptake is seen.
l: Which lymph node group received the tracer?
e: About 75 percent of breast lymph drains to the axilla, but the medial quadrants also drain along the internal thoracic vessels to the **internal mammary** (parasternal) nodes beside the sternum. A medial tumor can therefore send its sentinel node there. The axillary levels are named by their relation to pectoralis minor: level I is lateral to the muscle, level II behind it and level III medial to it. Supraclavicular nodes lie above the clavicle.

w.Level I axillary nodes: Level I nodes lie lateral to pectoralis minor in the lower armpit and receive most lateral-quadrant lymph. The scan showed no uptake there at all.
w.Level III (apical) axillary nodes: Level III (apical) nodes lie medial to pectoralis minor and are reached after levels I and II, so they are rarely the first stop.
w.Supraclavicular nodes: Supraclavicular nodes lie above the clavicle and receive lymph only after the axillary or parasternal chains. They are not a first stop.
w.Level II axillary nodes: Level II nodes lie behind pectoralis minor in the axilla. The scan showed no axillary uptake, so the tracer did not go there.

et: Beside the sternum, deep to intercostal spaces
Can be first for medial tumors
Medial to pectoralis minor, under the clavicle
bl: Medial-quadrant tumors can drain first to the internal mammary (parasternal) nodes along the internal thoracic vessels.

pt.say: At the top left, the internal mammary nodes drain the medial quadrants along the internal thoracic vessels beside the sternum.

s: A 55-year-old woman has a 1.5-cm invasive ductal carcinoma in the upper outer quadrant of her left breast and no palpable axillary nodes. Before lumpectomy, blue dye and radiotracer are injected near the areola. The surgeon removes the first blue, radioactive node in the lower axilla, and frozen section shows no tumor.
l: Which conclusion is best supported by this result?
o: Further axillary dissection can be omitted
Level III nodes must be sampled next
The internal mammary chain must be dissected
The tumor is confined by its basement membrane
e: Lymph from a tumor reaches the axillary nodes in order, so the first node on the path, the sentinel node, predicts the rest. A tumor-free sentinel node means the remaining axillary nodes are very unlikely to hold tumor, so **further axillary dissection can be omitted**. That spares the nerves and lymphatics at risk. Level III nodes are reached only after the lower levels. A negative node does not rule out spread through the blood to distant organs.

w.Level III nodes must be sampled next: Apical nodes lie beyond levels I and II on the drainage path. With a clean first node, spread to them is unlikely, so sampling them is unnecessary.
w.The internal mammary chain must be disse: Internal mammary nodes matter mainly for medial tumors. This tumor is in the upper outer quadrant, so that chain is not the concern.
w.Distant metastasis has been excluded: Carcinoma also spreads through the blood to bone, liver, lung and brain. A clean node lowers the likelihood of metastasis but cannot rule it out.
w.The tumor is confined by its basement me: An invasive ductal carcinoma has by definition already crossed its basement membrane. Node status reflects lymphatic spread, not whether invasion occurred.

et: Further axillary dissection can be omitted
Level III nodes must be sampled next
Spread through levels I and II first
The internal mammary chain must be dissected
Imaging of bone, liver, lung and brain
The tumor is confined by its basement membrane
bl: A tumor-free sentinel node predicts clean remaining nodes, so further axillary dissection can be omitted.

pt.say: The sentinel node, ringed at level I, is the first axillary stop; when it is clean, further axillary dissection can be skipped.

s: A 49-year-old woman who swims competitively had a right modified radical mastectomy with axillary node dissection 3 months ago. She now struggles to pull herself out of the pool and to reach into her back pocket with her right hand. Her scapula stays flat against the chest wall when she pushes against a wall, and light touch over the medial upper arm is normal.
l: Which nerve was most likely injured during the operation?
e: Pulling the body up and reaching into a back pocket need extension, adduction and internal rotation of the arm, which are the actions of latissimus dorsi. Its nerve, the **thoracodorsal nerve**, runs along the posterior axillary wall close to the nodes removed in a dissection. A long thoracic injury would wing the scapula, which is not seen here. An intercostobrachial injury would numb the medial arm, but her sensation is normal.

w.Long thoracic nerve: Loss of serratus anterior lets the medial border of the scapula lift off the ribs. Her scapula stays flat during a wall push, which rules this out.
w.Intercostobrachial nerve: Cutting this sensory T2 branch numbs the armpit and inner arm without weakness. Her sensation there is normal and her deficit is motor.
w.Lateral pectoral nerve: This nerve supplies the upper pectoralis major, which flexes and adducts the arm across the chest. Injury weakens pushing and hugging, not pulling down and back.
w.Axillary nerve: Deltoid and teres minor lose power after a humeral neck fracture or shoulder dislocation, which weakens abduction. Node surgery rarely reaches this nerve.

et: Flexion and adduction across the chest
Abduction beyond the first few degrees
bl: Weak extension and adduction with a flat scapula after axillary surgery means thoracodorsal nerve injury to latissimus dorsi.

pt.say: The middle card shows the thoracodorsal nerve to latissimus dorsi, whose injury weakens adduction and extension, her exact deficit.

s: A 30-year-old woman who is exclusively breastfeeding her 6-week-old son notices that milk begins to spray from both nipples whenever she hears him cry, even before he latches.
l: Contraction of which cells ejects the milk?
e: The cry triggers a conditioned reflex. The hypothalamus signals the posterior pituitary to release oxytocin, which binds receptors on the **myoepithelial cells** that wrap every alveolus and duct. Their contraction squeezes milk into the ducts and out of the nipple, the let-down reflex. Luminal epithelial cells make milk under prolactin but cannot contract, and lactotrophs secrete prolactin instead of ejecting milk.

w.Luminal epithelial cells: The inner luminal layer makes milk proteins and fat under prolactin and releases them into the lumen. It has no contractile filaments to push milk out.
w.Areolar smooth muscle cells: Smooth muscle in the areola and nipple contracts to erect the nipple. It does not surround the alveoli where milk is stored.
w.Intralobular stromal cells: The loose stroma around the lobules responds to hormones, but it has no contractile cells that could push milk out.
w.Anterior pituitary lactotrophs: Lactotrophs secrete prolactin, which keeps milk synthesis going between feeds. Ejection depends on oxytocin from the posterior pituitary.

et: Outer layer of alveoli and ducts
bl: Oxytocin makes the myoepithelial cells around alveoli contract, producing milk let-down.

s: A 54-year-old woman has a 1.2-cm spiculated density on screening mammography. Core biopsy shows irregular nests and small glands of atypical epithelial cells scattered through a dense fibrous stroma. Immunostains for p63 and smooth muscle myosin heavy chain are positive in a continuous rim around adjacent normal ducts but are absent around the atypical nests and glands.
l: What does the absent staining around the atypical glands indicate?
o: Loss of the myoepithelial layer from invasion
e: p63 and smooth muscle myosin mark **myoepithelial cells**. These cells normally form a continuous outer layer around ducts and lobules and still surround carcinoma in situ. Tumor cells that break through the basement membrane into the stroma form nests with no myoepithelial rim. Absent staining therefore means invasive carcinoma, which fits the spiculated mass. Sclerosing adenosis can also look infiltrative, but its compressed acini keep their myoepithelial layer and stain.

w.Sclerosing adenosis with compressed acin: This benign mimic distorts crowded acini with fibrosis, but every acinus keeps a continuous p63-positive rim. These nests lack that rim.
w.Lobular rather than ductal differentiati: Lobular carcinoma is recognized by loss of E-cadherin, not by myoepithelial stains. Both ductal and lobular in situ lesions keep a myoepithelial rim.
w.Overexpression of the HER2 receptor: HER2 status is read with a separate membrane stain or a gene amplification test. p63 and myosin say nothing about growth factor receptors.
w.Lactational change in the lobules: Lactating lobules show dilated alveoli with vacuolated cells and milk, and their contractile outer layer is preserved to eject that milk.

et: Loss of the myoepithelial layer from invasion
p63 and smooth muscle myosin negative
p63 and smooth muscle myosin positive
Present in the in situ phase
bl: Absent myoepithelial staining (p63, smooth muscle myosin) around tumor nests means the carcinoma is invasive.

s: A pathology resident reviews breast tissue from a 28-year-old woman who died in a car crash 8 weeks after delivering a healthy infant. The lobules are enlarged and packed with dilated alveoli lined by cuboidal cells with vacuolated cytoplasm. Electron microscopy shows lipid droplets bulging from the apical surface and pinching off wrapped in a thin layer of plasma membrane and cytoplasm.
l: Which secretory mechanism releases the milk component described?
e: Milk fat is released by **apocrine secretion**. The lipid droplet pushes against the apical membrane and pinches off with a thin rim of membrane and cytoplasm. Milk proteins such as casein leave the same cells by merocrine secretion, which is exocytosis of secretory vesicles with no loss of cytoplasm. Holocrine secretion, in which the whole cell breaks down, describes sebaceous glands.

w.Merocrine secretion: Exocytosis of vesicles releases milk proteins such as casein without losing any cell membrane, so it cannot explain membrane-wrapped fat droplets.
w.Holocrine secretion: Sebaceous glands release their product when the whole cell breaks down. Lactating alveolar cells survive and keep secreting.
w.Transcytosis: Transcytosis carries proteins such as IgA across the cell in vesicles. It does not release the membrane-wrapped fat droplets described.
w.Paracellular diffusion: Paracellular diffusion is leakage between cells. It does not wrap lipid in membrane the way these droplets are released.

et: How the product leaves the cell
Apex pinches off around the droplet
bl: Milk fat leaves alveolar cells by apocrine secretion. Milk proteins leave by merocrine exocytosis.

s: A 29-year-old woman at 36 weeks' gestation asks why her breasts, which have enlarged greatly during pregnancy, are not yet producing milk, even though her serum prolactin is many times the nonpregnant level. Two days after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery and expulsion of the placenta, her breasts become firm and full, and copious milk production begins.
l: The onset of copious milk production after delivery is best explained by a fall in which hormone?
e: During pregnancy, estrogen, **progesterone** and prolactin build the lobules and alveoli, but the very high placental progesterone blocks prolactin from switching on full milk synthesis. Delivery of the placenta removes that source, and the fall in progesterone over the next few days releases the brake. Copious milk then appears while prolactin stays high. A fall in prolactin would reduce milk, and oxytocin controls ejection, not production.

w.Prolactin: Prolactin stays high after delivery and rises further with each feeding. It drives milk synthesis, so a fall would stop lactation.
w.Oxytocin: Oxytocin surges during labor and suckling to make myoepithelial cells contract and eject milk. It moves milk that is already made.
w.Dopamine: Hypothalamic dopamine inhibits prolactin release, so less dopamine would raise prolactin. But prolactin was already high before delivery without copious milk.
w.Human placental lactogen: Human placental lactogen also falls after delivery. Its main roles are maternal insulin resistance and breast growth, and its loss does not unlock milk secretion.

et: Builds alveoli; blocks full milk synthesis
bl: Placental delivery drops progesterone, releasing its block on prolactin, so copious milk production begins.
